stories.title_en: Verification Is Not Knowledge: Science needs more than answers

comments.author: A_D_E_P_T
comments.text:
The article's perspective reminds me of math class when I was a kid.  The teacher didn't want the right answer alone, she wanted to see how I got there.  In an absolute sense, the right answer is the right answer with or without my understanding, but that's not how the class was graded.  We're approaching a point where AI is to science as my old calculator is to elementary school math -- it's capable of leapfrogging to answers faster and more accurately than we can.
Thing is, though, verification is knowledge itself.  And if we can get to a point where the important questions have answers, we can surely have the verifiers explain those to us in ways we can understand them.

comments.author: My_Name
comments.text:
Surely the way forwards is to take the results obtained by brute force with AI, for example that certain conjectures are true or false, then to use that knowledge to further human understanding.
Knowing that something is true or false will at least stop humans wasting time trying to prove or disprove it, and allow them to find a more elegant proof, or investigate the implications of the true/false result.

comments.text:
Back in 2018, when I was at Greenplum, my team worked through The Internals of PostgreSQL together alongside Andy Pavlo’s CMU database courses. It was invaluable for anyone working on the database kernel. Today, a beginner can get that same interactive learning experience simply by chatting with AI, much like the discussions our team had back then.
Now I’m building Lavik, a new cache service for PostgreSQL. Traditional caches like Redis are DRAM-based, so they can only hold a small slice of hot data. Once your data outgrows memory, you’re exposed to cache miss storms, where a flood of requests falls through to PostgreSQL all at once. Nobody likes those. (OpenAI encounter the similar cache miss storms problem:
https://openai.com/index/scaling-postgresql/
)
Lavik takes a different path: it runs on NVMe SSDs, and it’s still faster than Redis running on DRAM. That’s not what most people expect. Conventional wisdom says SSD-based systems trade speed for capacity, but Lavik gives you both. You can keep TB-scale data in cache while getting 1M QPS and sub-millisecond P99 latency.
Lavik is open source under the Apache License.
GitHub:
https://github.com/eloqdata/lavik
Website:
https://lavik

comments.text: Chapter 12 (full-text search) quietly changed under this book in Postgres 18: FTS now reads its dictionaries and config through the cluster's default collation provider instead of always libc, so clusters on ICU or the new builtin PG_UNICODE_FAST can see different behavior in FTS and pg_trgm — the release notes explicitly tell you to reindex those indexes after pg_upgrade. comments.author: getbrew
comments.text: The HOT chapter is the one with the most direct practical payoff. Two things worth knowing from it: HOT only kicks in when no indexed column changes and the new tuple fits on the same page, so an index on a frequently-updated column (status, updated_at) quietly disables it for every update to that table. And lowering fillfactor (say 80-90) on update-heavy tables leaves free space on each page so HOT can actually happen. Comparing n_tup_hot_upd to n_tup_upd in pg_stat_user_tables is a cheap way to see whether you're getting HOT updates before tuning anything.

stories.title_en: C++26 Disapproved

comments.author: jandrewrogers
comments.text:
As someone who writes high-reliability C++ but is completely outside the standards process, I see the issues with C++ Contracts. It isn’t clear that it solves a problem that anyone has in real codebases, especially after C++20 concepts.
If you were already writing high-reliability C++ then the benefits are difficult to quantify. If you weren’t writing high-reliability C++ then it saves you almost nothing over doing the standard idioms of high-reliability C++ that were already available to you at very marginally more cost. It
does
standardize expression of it in narrow cases but the payoff seems minimal.
Most of what C++ Contracts delivers is a mashup of what you can already do with constexpr and C++20 Concepts. I like reliability features but this feature, as delivered, looks fairly useless if you already use reliability features. A compelling standard would need to make much deeper guarantees out of the box. And the compiler can already see through most compositions of constexpr and C++20 concepts, which is already very expressive.
C++ Contracts looks a bit like a feature that was designed long before current standard features existed.

While I can understand that C++ contracts were met with controversy, contract annotations scoped at analysis time that can be verified by external tools, such as static analyzers, model checkers, or automatic theorem provers, are incredibly useful.
I put together an alternative function contract and invariant mechanism in C using CBMC and custom macros that effectively allows me to perform formal methods in C using compositional verification. The reason why I chose C is because of its relative simplicity and relative ease of building tooling around it. C++ contracts provide some feature parity, and would let me take advantage of some of the features in C++ relative to C.
I hope that the contract proposal is workshopped and simplified so it can be proposed again for a future version. Its current form is unsuitable, but it deserves a second chance with a simpler implementation. Contracts would narrow the safety gap between C++ and languages such as Ada / SPARK.

Anyone that's never had the (dis)pleasure of working with tapes, there's some gotchas to know about before archiving and forgetting about it.
When you create an archive, do not skip the step of reading it back. I'm not talking about just having the system confirm it is readable. I mean actually restoring the data from the tape. I've had tapes fail to retrieve data off of the tape even though the writing app confirmed it was readable.
Drives can have issues reading data written by another drive. Drives can have issues reading a tape it wrote itself.
Why write one when you can write two at twice the time/cost? In all of my experience with tape, I've never written just one tape. In the early days of DVDs, the images were written to LTO to send to have the discs pressed. comments.author: x313
comments.text:
I work in this field (mech interp research) and I agree, the original post is definitely misleading. Some overselling in research is normal but it's a bit much.
First, the key result has nothing to do with making Qwen better at math, it just reduces reasoning loops.
Reasoning loops are a simple problem: the model generates the </think> token (which closes reasoning) with too low probability. You can fix this with simple steering approaches where you add a vector to different components of the LLM (
https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.22048
,
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.18167
, etc). The method Astra used for identifying the vector is the standard procedure humans use (contrastive analysis). Such steering vector creation is basically the standard "intro-level interp project" for human researchers.
If you can code and understand LLM internals, you can do this yourself in 4-8 hours. The SWE equivalent would be doing binary patching with a debugger. Cool that frontier models can do this, but not unexpected since humans can do it without issue.
